questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: My interest in the culture and how it is to live there and improving my French

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: An amazing experience, but definitely tough at times

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy, as I had a contact person at Sorbonne whom I could email, and everything was handled in person or by email so I wasn't expected to search for any information on any websites.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: After my arrival, I emailed my academic Erasmus contact person at Sorbonne, who organised a meeting with two other academic administrative people where they helped me choose my courses in person. She also set up my Sorbonne email and Moodle (intranet) account. There was also an Erasmus welcome meeting for all the exchange students.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Cité universitaire! It is an international "city" of student houses each belonging to a country in the southernmost part of Paris. It is a great way to meet other international students, some of whom are doing a whole master's in Paris and are well integrated in Paris life, and some of whom are just Erasmus students. It's an experience in itself to live there, and the Danish house is a special place.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
There is no on-campus accommodation.
The decision is between living in student housing (kollegier) together with other students or living 'alone' in an apartment. Living alone in an apartment might give a more authentic experience of living in Paris (or not), but you have to put a lot more work into meeting people (which isn't impossible at all with all the cultural/student/social events happening in Paris).
There is also French student housing for French students that is also available to Erasmus students through Sorbonne when you apply, but it isn't so common for French students to live in student housing and it isn't necessarily so attractive.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
There was an online application process that included several short motivated letters, but most of it was just formalities.
After I had arrived in Paris, my Erasmus contact person at Sorbonne arranged a relaxed meeting with two other academic administrative people where they helped me choose my courses. They were teachers in some of the courses themselves or researchers at the university, so I could ask them questions about the courses. They took care of signing me up for the courses I had chosen and setting up my email and intranet account.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The administrative people present at the meeting were happy to answer questions and make suggestions about which courses I should take, and the whole meeting was about me choosing my courses.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I ended up with courses in areas I was interested in, but most of the courses I had chosen from home were only offered in the spring semester, so I couldn't take them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Notice which semester the courses are offered in.
Make a longer list of courses you could be interested in, in case there are schedule conflicts or canceled courses.
Be well prepared for any meetings, as you might have to decide on the spot.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Impressively many courses to choose between

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The neuroscience courses were very challenging and definitely at a high enough level for a 3rd year Mol. Bio. student, and they were especially ambitious with creating context for the neuroscience and connecting it to things I hadn't learnt about before, e.g. congnitive/behavioural science and philosophy.
As the education at Sorbonne is general Biology, the other students hadn't had as much molecular biology/ protein science, so in a subject such as Microbiologie, the level didn't feel so high, and they didn't go into as much depth with molecular cell biology or lab methods as I might have wished.
But everything was challenging due to the language (all courses were in French, including exams, and we were treated no different from the French students).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The courses at Sorbonne are either 6 ECTS or 3 ECTS, which means that you have 7 or 8 courses at the same time for the semester. This meant that the courses didn't go into as much depth as they do at KU, but there was still a lot of material covered in each course. Overall, the focus was more on learning a lot of information by heart than on learning a few key concepts in depth (with the exception of the math course I took at Sorbonne).
At the Sorbonne biology institute there is also a somewhat extreme amount of teaching; I could have up to 36 hours of teaching a week, but usually had around 26, which meant at least one to two 8-18 days each week and school every day.
The teachers had more power to decide, and they didn't always explain why we were learning something or tell us beforehand what the lecture would be about, which felt chaotic at times. However the lectures were often more inspiring and on more untraditional subjects or with a certain angle, because the teachers had more freedom in structuring their lectures, e.g. a fascinating lecture on neurophilosophy in a neuro course.
There were no books or reading material, so what the teachers said during the classes was the curriculum, and you were expected to absorb most things during lectures or TD (classroom teaching/exercises, which was repetition of the material from the lectures). But it was more acceptable/expected to ask questions during lectures, and sometimes the lecturer would start a discussion with a student and the lecture would even end up in that direction.
Overall I thought it was a positive experience to be so immersed in university life and see this more oral/dialogue-based approach to teaching.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Neurophysiologie et physiologie des grandes fonctions (6 ECTS)
Microbiologie (3 ECTS)
Biochimie: métabolisme (3 ECTS)
Mathématiques et statistiques pour la biologie (3 ECTS)
Francais langue étrangère (3 ECTS)
Physiopathologies humaines et stratégies de recherche (6 ECTS)
Cerveau et comportement (6 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Cerveau et comportement: fascinating lectures on subjects in neuroscience, e.g. emotions, addiction, philosophy of the brain, consciousness - by very competent lecturers.
Physiopathologies humaines et stratégies de recherche: interesting/useful course for mol. bio., as each lecture was on a different illness that was treated as a case and that we learnt about in depth, including the social background of the illness and the progress of research. The classroom teaching was practice reading and presenting papers about each illness.
Microbiologie: a well-organised and interesting and inspiring course, even though it didn't go into as much depth as I might have wished.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
Having to buy single train tickets after having lost my monthly train card
When in very touristy areas, watch out for people trying to trick you into giving them a lot of money, e.g. the tourist rickshaws.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Some things in the supermarkets could be randomly priced, so you had to watch out.
Baguettes were very cheap :)
Sports/gyms are expensive
Most museums are free if you're under 26.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Sorbonne offered relatively many sports classes at campus that seemed reasonably priced, but I didn't use any of them as I used the sports offered in Cité Universitaire. 
Parismus, a student organisation whose aim is to connect foreign students and French students, organised many events, from walks to parties and picnics and museum visits. E.g. Apérismus, which was a popular Wednesday bar (instead of a Friday bar) every second Wednesday.
There were many other student organisations, e.g. a philosophy club that organised philosophy film viewings with discussions afterwards.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Anything that Parismus organises, as it is an easy way to meet French students interested in meeting exchange students, or to meet other exchange students.
There is so much going on in Paris and so many students and cultural institutions etc., so find whatever interests you!
French cinemas, cafés, (book)shopping, just exploring and enjoying Paris !

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Don't be afraid to do all the touristy things.
The nightlife in Paris should be experienced

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Sometimes difficult, especially in the beginning, but with an open mind it was fine.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Speak French :o)
Just go for it, most people are very willing to talk to people they don't know and help each other with notes etc.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Chaos, over-complicated ways of dealing with some things and general dysfunctioning of e.g. the metro.
The subtleties of French culture can be different from the Danish and can be difficult to get into straight away, but you can't expect to become French from living there for 5 months, sometimes you are just the clueless Erasmus student.
People, e.g. university staff can sometimes seem agressive and volatile, and conflicts are more common and less serious.
Spontaneity and the French way of being polite which sometimes requires a lot of alertness and quick thinking in the most unlikely situations.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
Spontaneity and how you can do so many things without planning beforehand, and talk to so many people, the love of discussions.
The more lively student life.
The inexhaustible energy French/Parisian people seem to have

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Take what happens at university with a pinch of salt, and focus on what you want to get out of the university experience instead of what the professors expect or the general atmosphere of stress around tests and presentations.
Be patient with learning the language and speak/make mistakes.
Be brave and do whatever you want to while on exchange!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: no

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
Improving my French so much
Meeting so many new people
Creating a life in Paris

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Balancing school work with social life at the student accommodation and exploring Paris and looking after myself.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: no

questions.answer: Yes
